rows.summary: A joint mission by an Indian Air Force helicopter crew and a Nepalese army medical team delivered tents, medicines and food to Melamchi, a remote village about a 44km drive from Kathmandu, on only the third such operation to reach it since Saturday's 7.8-magnitude earthquake killed more than 5,000 people. According to Nepal's National Emergency Operation Center, Sindhupalchok District, which includes Melamchi, suffered 1,376 deaths. Local official Upendra Tamang said about 18,000 homes had been destroyed and 100,000 people displaced in the surrounding area, with everyone sleeping outdoors. He warned that the food delivered was inadequate and urged aid agencies to act quickly. Tamang said around 500 of the most seriously injured had already been sent to Kathmandu, mostly by road, while many others remained at a local clinic awaiting help. The helicopter evacuated seven patients—five women and two men—whose injuries were not life-threatening but who appeared exhausted and traumatized. Among them was Forshani Tamang, whose son said relatives had carried her for four hours from Bachunde, where nearly all homes were destroyed. Her family had lost its house and grain supplies. Nepalese army doctor Naveen Tiwari said the patients mainly had lacerations, their vital signs were stable, and they should recover with antibiotics and intravenous fluids. At Kathmandu airbase, paramedics treated the patients while the relief team prepared for another mission.

Director J.J. Abrams and the cast unveiled a 110-second trailer for "Star Wars: Episode VII -- The Force Awakens" at an enthusiastically received Anaheim event, with Harrison Ford's return as Han Solo alongside Chewbacca drawing an emotional response; the film is scheduled for December 18. Abrams identified the desert planet as Jakku, where Rey meets stormtrooper Finn, and highlighted the use of real sets and a physical BB-8 droid, while the trailer also featured Luke's voice and remnants of the Empire.

Delhi (CNN)An international human rights group is calling for an independent investigation of the killings by police of 20 suspected red sandalwood smugglers in southeastern India. According to Amnesty, India's National Human Rights Commission has said the incident "involved a serious violation of human rights of the individuals," and that "the opening of firing cannot be justified on the ground of self defense since it resulted in the loss of lives of 20 persons." The commission has asked senior government and police officials to explain the actions of the police and forest officials within two weeks, Amnesty said.
